prompt: By the lesson, what is a work document judged by?
hint: It is a tool for somebody else.

choices.text: Whether it follows the company template
choices.why: A template can help, but a document that follows it and leaves the reader not knowing what to do has still failed.

choices.text: Its length, which shows how seriously the work was taken
choices.why: Length is a cost imposed on every reader, and the reader cannot tell from it whether the extra pages carry anything.

choices.text: Whether the reader takes the action it was written for
choices.why: Right: a document exists for the reader's next step, and it worked if that step happens.

choices.text: How much of the investigation it records
choices.why: That organises the document around the writer, which is the habit the lesson starts by naming.

prompt: Lívia cannot say what the finance director should do after reading her note. What does the lesson call such a document?
hint: The third of the four questions.

choices.text: A diary entry
choices.why: Right: with no answer to "what should they do?", it records the writer's thinking and asks nothing of the reader.

choices.text: A draft that needs a template
choices.why: A template does not supply the missing action; only the writer can.

choices.text: A message for the skimmer rather than the reader
choices.why: Skimming is about how a document is read, not about whether it asks anything.

choices.text: A document for an audience of three different people
choices.why: That is the first question going wrong, a reader who is really three readers, which is a different problem.

prompt: A status note goes to 30 people and takes each of them 5 minutes to decode. How many minutes of other people's time did it cost in total?
Why does Lívia's note to Caio end with "You do not need to do anything yet"?
hint: Think about what a finance director does with a vague warning.

choices.text: To hide how serious the problem is
choices.why: The note gives the size of the problem plainly, 180 customers a week; nothing is hidden.

choices.text: It answers what he should do, so he does not reply with questions
choices.why: Right: "nothing yet" is an answer to "what should they do?", and without it a reader in his position starts asking.

choices.text: To be polite, because he is more senior than her in the company
choices.why: It is courteous, but the sentence is there because it answers the third question for this reader.

choices.text: Because the decision belongs to the checkout team and not to finance
choices.why: The note says a proposal is coming to a meeting he attends; it is not handing the decision away.

prompt: What does BLUF ask of the first lines of a message?

choices.text: What the reader must know or do
choices.why: Right: everything below the first lines is support for them.

choices.text: A summary of the previous message in the thread
choices.why: A recap repeats what the reader read; BLUF puts the new thing first.

choices.text: A greeting and the context of the work so far
choices.why: That is the run-up BLUF exists to remove; the context goes below the point, if anywhere.

choices.text: The evidence, so the conclusion is believed when it arrives
choices.why: Evidence first is the investigation order, and a busy reader stops before the conclusion.

prompt: Under one governing idea Lívia lists: "it loses sales", "it can stop checkout" and "migrate the route planner on Tuesday". What is wrong?
hint: The second rule of the pyramid.

choices.text: The arguments should come before the governing idea
choices.why: That reverses the pyramid; the idea is at the top so the reader can stop there.

choices.text: Two reasons and a step are not the same kind of thing
choices.why: Right: arguments at one level are all reasons, all steps or all options. The step belongs elsewhere.

choices.text: There should be exactly four arguments
choices.why: There is no fixed number; three is common, two strong ones are fine.

choices.text: "It can stop checkout" is only a guess
choices.why: A risk is a legitimate argument when its evidence sits under it, as the figure shows.

prompt: Which subject line lets a reader decide whether the message is theirs without opening it?
hint: What it is for, by when and at what cost.

choices.text: Friday checkout
choices.why: It says the topic and nothing about what is wanted from the reader.

choices.text: Some thoughts on our database situation after last week's Friday problems in checkout
choices.why: "Some thoughts" warns the reader that there is no ask, so it waits for a free moment that does not come.

choices.text: Decision needed by 19 March: separate the route planner (6 engineer-weeks)
choices.why: Right: the ask, the date and the cost are all in the line.

choices.text: URGENT: please read
choices.why: Urgency with no content makes the reader open it to find out what it is, which is the cost the subject line should save.

prompt: Lívia must tell Henrique that the plan he championed will not work. By the lesson, what should the first lines of her note do?
hint: The exception to the answer coming first.

choices.text: State bluntly that the plan fails, because BLUF has no exceptions
choices.why: The lesson names this exact case as one where a reader rejects a conclusion met before its reasons.

choices.text: Open with praise for the plan to soften the reader up
choices.why: Padding before bad news is still padding, and the reader notices the shape.

choices.text: Tell the story of the investigation in the order it happened
choices.why: Walking through reasons is not the same as a chronological diary; the reader still gets told what the note is for.

choices.text: Say what it is for, then give the reasons before the verdict
choices.why: Right: the reader still knows where the document is going, and meets the reasons before the verdict.

prompt: Match each vague phrase to the precise version from the lesson's table.
hint: Each precise version can be checked.

pairs.right: Bruna is testing the fix; next update at 16:00

prompt: An engineer writes "the migration will take 13.5 days" when the real estimate is two to four weeks. What has gone wrong?
hint: More digits than the estimate deserves.

choices.text: It should have said "soon", so that nobody holds the team to a date
choices.why: That swaps false precision for vagueness; the lesson asks for the range.

choices.text: Nothing: a single number is always clearer for the reader than a range
choices.why: Clearer to read and wrong to plan on; precision is about matching what you know.

choices.text: False precision: people will plan on a confidence nobody has
choices.why: Right: a range stated honestly, with when it will narrow, is the precise version here.

choices.text: Days are the wrong unit for a migration
choices.why: The unit is fine; the trouble is the half-day of precision nobody has.

prompt: A design document calls the same system "the orders database", "Postgres" and "the core store". What does a newcomer conclude?

choices.text: That the author writes with pleasing variety
choices.why: Variety is a school-essay virtue; in technical prose it creates systems that do not exist.

choices.text: Nothing, because everybody knows these are synonyms
choices.why: Everybody who already knows the system; the newcomer is exactly the reader who does not.

choices.text: That Postgres is replacing the orders database
choices.why: A plausible guess, and the kind of wrong conclusion the shifting names invite.

choices.text: That there are three different systems
choices.why: Right: a second name reads as a second thing. Define one name and keep it.

prompt: "Perform an analysis of the logs" becomes "___ the logs".
hint: The verb hiding inside the noun.

prompt: How many words did Lívia cut from the 86-word paragraph to reach the version she kept?
Which of these edits takes economy too far?
hint: The test: would a reader lose anything?

choices.text: Turning "it seems that it could possibly be related to" into "it may be related to"
choices.why: Three hedges become one, and the uncertainty is still stated.

choices.text: Rewriting "the deploy was approved" as "Bruna approved the deploy" in the release notes
choices.why: That adds a name rather than cutting one, and the name was the point.

choices.text: Deleting "As some of you may be aware" from the opening
choices.why: Throat-clearing; nobody loses anything.

choices.text: Cutting "because the primary is the bottleneck at peak" from "use the replica"
choices.why: Right: the reason is what stops the next person undoing the change, and it is exactly what a reader would lose.

prompt: Put the six editing passes in the lesson's order.
hint: Structure before sentences, and a real reader last.
items: Write the point in one sentence
Read only the headings and first sentences
Cut what the reader would not miss
Check every number, name and date
Ask one real reader what you are asking
trap: Polishing sentences before the structural passes wastes work on paragraphs that are about to be deleted.

prompt: In pass 6, what single question does Lívia ask her test reader?
hint: It checks the document against pass 1.

choices.text: "Are all the numbers and dates in it correct?"
choices.why: That is pass 4, and the writer checks it against the sources, not by asking.

choices.text: "What do you think I am asking you to do?"
choices.why: Right: if the answer is not the sentence from pass 1, the document failed however well it reads.

choices.text: "Did you enjoy reading it?"
choices.why: Enjoyment does not tell her whether the ask came across.

choices.text: "Is there anything I should cut?"
choices.why: Useful, but the cut was pass 3; pass 6 tests whether the document worked.

prompt: Lívia's draft says: "Hi all, hope the weekend was good! Following on from various discussions, I've been thinking about database access and would like each team to look at things sometime." Which changes does the lesson call for? Choose all that apply.
hint: Point first, precise ask, cut the run-up.

choices.text: Open with the ask: each team sends its peak connections
choices.why: Yes: the point in the first line.

choices.text: Add a paragraph on how the database was chosen in 2019
choices.why: No reader needs that to act; it lengthens the message without helping anybody do anything.

choices.text: Replace "sometime" with a date
choices.why: Yes: a deadline the reader can check.

choices.text: Cut the greeting and "following on from various discussions"
choices.why: Yes: throat-clearing, which carries nothing.

prompt: Before sending a chat message, the six passes collapse into one question. Which?
hint: From the section on how long editing takes.

choices.text: Would this be better as a meeting?
choices.why: Sometimes true, but not the question the lesson asks before pressing enter.

choices.text: Have I been polite enough?
choices.why: Courtesy matters, and it is not the question the lesson keeps.

choices.text: Is the point in the first line?
choices.why: Right: the one check that survives when there is no time for six.

choices.text: Have I attached every piece of evidence?
choices.why: Evidence goes below the point; a message is not improved by carrying all of it.

prompt: A proposal has a section headed "Costs". Following the lesson, what should the heading say instead?
hint: A heading has to survive the skim.

choices.text: The fix costs six engineer-weeks and R$ 4,000 a month
choices.why: Right: a skimmer who reads only the heading gets the claim.

choices.text: Nothing: headings are labels and the claim goes in the paragraph
choices.why: That is the habit the lesson asks to break, because the skimmer reads the heading and leaves.

choices.text: Costs, with the full breakdown in the appendix at the end
choices.why: Still a label, now pointing elsewhere; the skimmer learns nothing.

choices.text: Section 4: financial considerations
choices.why: Longer and still a label: it names a topic and makes no claim.
